title: Palindrome Linked List
description: Brute force to optimized: copying values to an array versus finding the middle, reversing the second half, and comparing directly.

blocks.text: Given the head of a singly linked list, return true if it is a PALINDROME (reads the same forward and backward).

blocks.caption: Find the middle, reverse the second half, then compare both halves directly

blocks.text: Given a linked list, determine whether its sequence of values reads the same forward and backward.

blocks.title: Analogy: Checking a Word for Being a Palindrome by Folding the Word in Half
blocks.text: Like checking whether a word is a palindrome by physically folding a strip of paper with the word written on it exactly in half, then checking whether the letters on each half line up when read together. Finding the fold point (the middle), physically flipping the second half over (reversing it), and then comparing the two halves letter by letter achieves the check directly, without needing a mirror or a second copy of the word.

blocks.caption: After reversing the second half, both halves can be walked forward together and compared directly

blocks.text: Before copying every value into an array to compare it against its own reverse, notice that the SECOND HALF of the list can be reversed in place, turning the whole problem into a simple forward comparison of two halves.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A linked list only supports forward traversal, so directly comparing "the first node" against "the last node" (and working inward) isn't naturally possible without some transformation first.

Observation 2: Using the classic slow/fast pointer technique locates the middle of the list in a single pass, exactly as in Middle of the Linked List.

Observation 3: Reversing just the SECOND HALF of the list, starting from that middle point, turns what would be a "walk backward" comparison into a simple "walk forward from both halves' respective starts" comparison instead.

Observation 4: Walking the original first half and the now-reversed second half together, node by node, comparing values at each step, directly checks the palindrome property; if every pair matches, the list is a palindrome.

Recognizing that reversing just half of the list (rather than needing random or backward access) converts an awkward backward-comparison problem into a simple forward one is the key insight that enables an O(1) space solution.
This combines two already-familiar techniques: the slow/fast pointer middle-finding technique, and the iterative in-place list reversal technique, applied to just the second half.
Copy every value into a plain array, then check whether the array reads the same forward and backward.

items: Walk through the list once, collecting every node's value into an array.
Use two pointers from both ends of the array, moving inward, comparing values at each step.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Values are collected first, since the two-pointer palindrome check needs random access to compare positions from both ends, which a linked list alone doesn't support.
Two pointers move inward from both ends of the array, the standard palindrome-checking technique for a random-access sequence.
The function returns false immediately upon the first mismatch, avoiding unnecessary further comparisons.

blocks.text: Every value is collected and compared correctly, so the palindrome check is always accurate.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to collect values plus one pass to compare.
Space: O(n), for the intermediate array holding every value.

Limitation: copying every value into an array to gain random access ignores that the second half of the list can instead be reversed in place, achieving the same comparison using only O(1) extra space.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force copies every value into an array. Instead, first find the middle of the list using slow/fast pointers. Then reverse the second half of the list in place (the same technique as Reverse Linked List, just starting partway through). Finally, walk the original first half and the newly-reversed second half together from their respective starts, comparing values at each step; if every pair matches, the list is a palindrome.

Use slow/fast pointers to find the middle of the list. Reverse the list starting from the middle node, using the standard iterative reversal technique. Then compare the original head (first half) and the new reversed-half head, walking both forward together and checking that every corresponding value matches.
Find the middle, reverse the second half in place, then walk both halves forward together comparing values.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: Since every compared pair matched, the answer is true, confirming the list is a palindrome.

codes.python:
def is_palindrome(head):
    slow = head
    fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next                                                   # find the middle using the classic slow/fast technique
        fast = fast.next.next

    prev = None
    curr = slow
    while curr:
        next_node = curr.next
        curr.next = prev                                                  # reverse the second half of the list in place
        prev = curr
        curr = next_node

    first, second = head, prev
    while second:                                                          # walk both halves together, comparing values
        if first.val != second.val:
            return False
        first = first.next
        second = second.next
    return True


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(2, ListNode(1))))
    print(is_palindrome(head))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), across finding the middle, reversing the second half, and comparing, each an O(n) pass.
Space: O(1) extra, reusing the existing nodes and only a handful of pointer variables.

Finding the middle via slow/fast pointers correctly splits the list into two halves (with the exact split point handled consistently for both even and odd lengths). Reversing the second half turns it into a sequence that, if the original list were a palindrome, would read IDENTICALLY to the first half when walked forward from each half's own start. Comparing the two halves node by node then directly verifies (or refutes) the palindrome property.

items: The middle-finding step is identical to Middle of the Linked List's slow/fast pointer technique.
The reversal step is identical to Reverse Linked List's iterative prev/curr/next technique, just applied starting from the middle node instead of the head.
The comparison loop is bounded by second (the shorter or equal-length reversed half), correctly handling both even- and odd-length original lists without needing separate cases.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Check if a linked list is a palindrome, using O(1) space" points toward finding the middle, reversing the second half in place, then comparing both halves via forward traversal.

items: How would you restore the list to its original order afterward? Reverse the second half back again (using the same reversal technique) once the comparison is complete, undoing the temporary modification.

How would you solve this using recursion instead? A recursive approach can implicitly use the call stack to "walk backward" while a separate forward pointer advances, though this uses O(n) space via the recursion stack instead of O(1).

What if the list were doubly linked instead of singly linked? A doubly linked list supports backward traversal directly, letting two pointers start from each end and move inward without any reversal step needed at all.

Directly combines the slow/fast pointer technique from Middle of the Linked List with the iterative reversal technique from Reverse Linked List, both elsewhere in this category, demonstrating how foundational techniques compose into harder problems.
